title: CLAY CITY VILLAGE BOARD MEETS
full_story:
The Clay City Village Board met Tuesday evening and wrestled with a variety of issues and took action to help a local businesswoman get started with a new business.

Mayor Mike Delonshaw called the meeting to order, and trustees quickly approved the past meeting minutes and the bills.  He then moved on to welcome visitors and heard from Damon Simmons, the owner of DBS Disposal, the company that provides trash pick up in several communities in the area.  Simmons asked to speak to the board because he is selling his business to Steve Stortzum of Louisville.  He said Clay City is one of the communities that its contract language stipulates that the village must approve the sale.  He stressed that nothing would change and he will remain with the company for a few months at least.  Mayor Delonshaw asked if any trustee had any problem granting approval and no one objected.  The mayor said the only problem is that the topic was not on the agenda and therefore the board couldn’t act on his request.  Simmons expressed disappointment about the possibility of having to wait another month to get their approval as it would negatively impact the transaction which is set for August 3rd.  Members then suggested they have a special meeting to accommodate Simmons.  He was grateful for their gesture and a motion was approved to hold a special meeting on Monday, July 13 at 4:00pm.

Next, Ali Hilderbrand addressed the board seeking to purchase a lot in Clay City to open a new beauty shop in Clay City.  The business is Ali’s Beauty Barn, which will be located at 800 Kelly Drive, behind Casey’s.  She explained that she is already in business offering hair products and is anxious to launch this new business in the coming months.  She stated that she intends to place a 16’ x 48’ building on the lot with a concrete foundation.  With the village always happy to see new businesses in town, trustees voted unanimously to sell her the property at a low cost of $10, and waives the cost of fees and utility hookups.  The agreement will include a stipulation that if the business is not still operating after three years, the village will reclaim ownership of the property.

Mayor Delonshaw stated that the village needs to purchase a truck to replace one that has failed and is unserviceable.  He stated he had contacted Eagleson Auto in Olney about purchasing a fleet vehicle and can accept a snowplow attachment and they have one available for about $41,000.  There was also discussion about possibly purchasing two trucks, but it remains unclear whether they will seek two vehicles.  Jim Duff suggested asking other dealers in the area and what they might offer and the issue was tabled until the next meeting.  Delonshaw went on to discuss making a change to the village ordinance that deals with the fees charged to new customers that would need to have utilities extended to their property.  The current ordinance lays out how the fee is figured but doesn’t specifically state what the fee should be.  The mayor suggested they simplify it and include figures.  That issue was also tabled and they’ll gather the figures for the next meeting.  Before moving on, Mayor Delonshaw pointed out that they made needed repairs to the electric service at the ballfields after power lines were damaged.  Trustees acknowledged that repairs were needed and it became an urgent repair when the damage occurred.  The work was performed at a cost of $12,000.

Brandon Bridges with Charleston Engineering of Olney presented a proposal to upgrade the South Pump House.  He said there were two bids, with the lower one coming in at under $141,000.  Trustee Sue Lindeman questioned the price and stated that when they talked about it earlier, the cost was around $80,000.  The mayor said that was only for the cost to upgrade the pumps and not the whole pump house.  He said once they replace the bladder, it has been operating as intended and is not constantly running.  Trustees Jim Duff and Larry Phillips suggested if its operating like it should, they should not take any further action at this time, especially with the looming purchase of new trucks or other items.

The agenda called for discussion and action on the Appropriations Ordinance and consideration of the Tax Levy.  Trustees questioned the need for action at this time and suggested they wait until later in the year, with a deadline near the end of the calendar year.  So the measure was tabled until a later date.

Before the meeting drew to a close, Clerk Shannon Hall asked for motion to approve the closure of Main St. for the Fall Festival on October 2nd and 3rd and the measure was quickly approved.  The mayor stated the board will need to act soon about whether to purchase it’s leased backhoe or lease another.  Utilities Superintendent Sean Sullens was asked how many hours the backhoe has on it and he replied not a lot.  It was then suggested that perhaps the village might purchase it and then sell it for more that they have in it and then lease another one, but no action was taken.  The mayor stated he had received a request from Kim Travis to purchase the lot next to her property.  Since that area is part of the drainage system, no construction can occur on it and consensus was that the village is not interested in selling the property.  The board will look into take action on nuisance properties and will consider that and other matters at the special meeting on Monday at 4:00pm at the village hall.  With business complete the meeting adjourned.

title: CCH SPORTS PHYSICALS
full_story:
The Clay County Hospital is offering free sports physicals for the next school year.

The next opportunity for a free sports physical is this afternoon, at the Flora Clinic, then tomorrow at the Louisville Clinic from 4 to 6 pm.  The final free sports physicals clinic will be held on Tuesday, at the Flora Clinic.  Wabash General Hospital athletic trainers will be at the clinics to assess athlete’s injury risk.

Appointments are not needed; physicals will be done on a first-come first-serve basis.

title: JULY BLOOD DRIVES
full_story:
ImpactLife will be having a blood drive at the Clay County Hospital tomorrow, from 10 am to 1 pm.  To schedule an appointment at this drive go to https://login.bloodcenter.org/donor/schedules/drive_schedule/144076

Every donation ears rewards.  Donors can chose between a $20 e-gift card, points to the Rewards Store, or donate the gift card to your favorite charity.

The American Red Cross is also making an urgent call for blood donors to book an appointment to give now to ensure hospitals stay ready to help patients without delay.

There will be a blood drive on Friday, from 1 to 5 pm at the Clay County Health Department.  All donors who donate blood during this drive will get a American Red Cross Looney Tunes T-shirt.  Then there will be a Blood Drive at the Flora Oddfellows Lodge on Friday July 24th from 1 to 5 pm.  Donors at this drive will get a Fandango Movie Reward by email.

Donors, especially those with type O blood and those giving platelets, can help bolster the blood supply now by making an appointment to give in the coming weeks.  You can make an appointment to donate at Red Cross Blood Drives by downloading the free Red Cross Blood Donor App, visiting redcrossblood.org or calling 1-800-RED CROSS (1-800-733-2767).  Save time with RapidPass.  Complete your pre-donation reading and health history at RedCrossBlood.org/RapidPass or with the Blood Donor App before your appointment.

title: OLNEY HOMICIDE
full_story:
The Olney Police Department and Richland County Sheriff’s Office requested the Illinois State Police’s (ISP) investigate two homicides in Olney.

On Tuesday, at approximately 3:11 pm, officers responded to two homes in the 400 block of East Monroe Street in Olney.  Officers found two deceased individuals in separate homes, 52-year-old John D. Jones Jr., and 73-year-old Deborah J. Jones.  One person is in custody and there is no risk to the public.

This is an ongoing investigation and no additional information is available at this time.

title: TYSON SCHULTE CONCERT
full_story:
Fairfield Memorial Hospital is proud to announce its sponsorship of the Tyson Schulte Concert following the Wayne County Agricultural Fair Rodeo tomorrow night.

As a longtime supporter of community events and local traditions, Fairfield Memorial Hospital is excited to sponsor an evening of live country music to fairgoers.  Following the rodeo, attendees are invited to stay and enjoy a performance by rising country artist Tyson Schulte, making Thursday night one of the highlights of this year’s fair.

“At Fairfield Memorial Hospital, we believe strong communities are built through opportunities to come together,” said Andy Flemer, CEO of Fairfield Memorial Hospital.  “The Wayne County Agricultural Fair has been a cherished tradition for generations, and we’re honored to sponsor Tyson Schulte’s performance.  We encourage everyone to come out, enjoy the fair, and make lasting memories with family and friends.”

title: SUSPECT IDENTIFIED
full_story:
Illinois State Police Tuesday confirmed the identity of the Effingham Church shooting on Sunday morning as 36-year-old Allen O. Gattino of St. Charles, Missouri.

Authorities say security at St. John’s Lutheran Church contacted Effingham Police on Sunday to report a suspicious man inside the church wishing to speak with the pastor.  Officers located Allen Gattino and learned he arrived in a vehicle that was reported stolen out of Marion County.  While trying to restrain Gattino he produced a gun and he was shot.  St. John’s cancelled services on Sunday.

As of their latest press release, this investigation is ongoing and more information will continue to come over the next days.

title: FREE KIDS FISHING DERBY
full_story:
State Representative Adam Niemerg is hosting his 4th Annual Free Kids Fishing Derby for children ages 4 to 15 on Saturday, July 25th.  The event will be held at the White Oak Shelter at the Sam Parr State Fish & Wildlife Area, located on Route 33 north of Newton.

“I am excited to once again host this popular event for families at Sam Parr Lake in my district,” said Niemerg.  “Parents, grandparents, and other relatives bring their children out for some fun and fresh air while getting away from computers, TV screens, and other electronics to learn how to fish for the first time.  Many also enjoy competing for trophies for the ‘Biggest Fish’ and ‘Most Fish’ caught that day.”

The event runs from 9:00 to 11:30 am and will include information about water safety, how to bait a hook, and how to reel in a fish.  In addition to awards for the biggest fish and most fish caught, there will also be drawings for other prizes.

Participants should enter the Sam Parr State Fish & Wildlife Area from Route 33 and proceed to the White Oak Shelter after the second right turn.  Follow the Fishing Derby signs.

Constituents may contact Representative Niemerg’s district office at 217-813-6036 or visit RepNiemerg.com with any questions.

title: DETAILS OF DISMEMBERMENT CASE
full_story:
Newly released court documents paint a deeply disturbing picture of the alleged killing and dismemberment of 38-year-old Dalewayne Turner of Plainfield, whose arm was discovered by boaters in Lake Mattoon on Sunday, June 28th.

Turner’s wife, Robin Turner, 62, and his half-brother, James Adams, 26, have been charged with concealment of a homicide and dismembering a human body.  Both remain in custody, and additional charges are likely to come.

According to court documents, the alleged killing took place around June 21st, at the home the three shared in Plainfield.  Robin Turner told police that on that Sunday, Dalewayne and Adams had a verbal argument over sports cards before Dalewayne said he was going to stay with a friend in Kankakee.  When she returned home, he was gone, but she now noticed a faint smell of bleach.

Adams allegedly told Turner’s brother that Dalewayne had entered the home and become physically violent.  Adams claimed he grabbed a knife and stabbed Turner multiple times.  According to the brother, the pair were initially unsure what to do, and that was when they decided to dismember the body and store it in a freezer.

The trail of evidence began to pile up just days later.  Surveillance cameras caught the pair at a Menards in Crest Hill, Illinois on June 23rd, purchasing 20 bags of concrete.  On June 26th, cameras in Mahomet picked up the truck with two duct-taped tote bags in the bed.  About 45 minutes later in Mattoon, those totes were gone.  Those same totes were later recovered less than a mile from where Turner’s partial remains had been found.

On the night of June 28th, Adams seemingly went to the Mattoon Walmart, where surveillance footage shows him purchasing weights, duct tape, and a change of clothes.  Adams can then be seen changing in the bathroom and discarding his old clothes in a dumpster.  Those same clothes were recovered from the dumpsters.

The case broke open on the evening of June 30th when Turner’s own brother called 911 after the pair told him what had happened.

Officers followed the truck to Munster, Indiana and back to Plainfield, conducted a traffic stop and detained both suspects.  When Adams was interviewed at the station, he reportedly invoked his right to remain silent.

A search warrant was then issued for the home the three shared on July 1st, investigators found the downstairs freezer had been duct taped shut, covered with a blanket, and weighed down with cinder blocks.  Inside, they found Turner’s torso, head, and neck.  An additional twist to the case came when Turner’s cell phone was recovered from the truck.

Robin Turner’s phone revealed text exchanges with Adams discussing dollies and cleaning supplies.  One message allegedly from Robin stated, “be sure to fully delete everything.”  Her Google history on that same phone dating back to June 2nd included searches about: overdose deaths, whether a body needs to be embalmed, and “concrete mixer,” among others linked to hiding the long-deceased body of her husband.

Tips from the public ultimately helped confirm the remains belonged to Turner and led to the arrest of his wife Robin and half-brother James.

A Will County judge ordered the suspects held until the case goes to trial.
